html:
The great oval amphitheatre in the centre of Rome, begun by Vespasian around 72 CE and opened by his son Titus in 80 CE. It is the largest amphitheatre ever built and the best-known symbol of ancient Rome.

Vespasian built it on the site of the lake of Nero's Golden House, giving land a tyrant had taken back to the people as a place of entertainment. An inscription suggests it was paid for with the spoils of the Jewish war (see Romans destroy the Second Temple). Built of stone, brick and concrete, it held around 50,000 spectators, seated by rank. Sailors stretched a huge awning over it on hot days. Domitian added the underground passages and lifts that brought animals and scenery up into the arena.

Titus opened it with a hundred days of games. It hosted gladiator fights, wild beast hunts and public executions. Gladiator fights ended in the 5th century and hunts in the 6th.

Earthquakes damaged it, and for centuries it was used as a quarry for stone. Even so, the north side of the outer wall still stands to its full height, and it inspired later arenas and stadiums worldwide.
